t.1.85.1: When you dwelt in Nandana, taking any form at will, for ten thousand hundreds of years, for what reason, O foremost of the Kṛta age, did you leave that and come down to the earth?
t.1.85.2: Just as here on earth a kinsman, friend, or one's own relative is abandoned by men once his wealth is spent, so there the hosts of gods, together with their lord, at once abandon the man whose merit is exhausted.
t.1.85.3: How do they become those whose merit is exhausted in that world? My mind is utterly bewildered on this point. Distinguished by what, to whose abode do they go? Tell me that, for I regard you as a knower of the field.
t.1.85.4: All of them, O lord of men, fall wailing into this earthly hell; there, though wasted away, they grow again in many ways, to become food for herons, jackals and crows.
t.1.85.5: Therefore a man should shun this deed, which is wicked and blameworthy in the world. All this has been told to you, O king; now tell me further, what more shall I tell you?
t.1.85.6: But when birds, vultures, blue-necked birds and other winged creatures tear at them, how do they survive, and how do they come into being again? I have never heard of any other hell upon the earth.
t.1.85.8: For sixty thousand and also eighty thousand years they fall through the sky, and as they plunge down the precipice, terrible earthly Rākṣasas with sharp fangs tear at them.
t.1.85.7: After leaving the body, driven by their karma as it unfolds, they wander visibly over the earth; they fall into this earthly hell and take no notice of the many multitudes of years that pass.
t.1.85.9: When those terrible earthly Rākṣasas with sharp fangs torment the sinful ones as they fall, how do these come to be, how do they come into existence again, and in what state do they become embryos?
t.1.85.11: They enter the trees and the plants, the waters, the wind, the earth and the intermediate space, and every four-footed and two-footed creature; having become thus, they become embryos.
t.1.85.10: The fluid follows the seed, mingled with flowers and fruits, that is emitted by the man; he then reaches her menstrual blood, and, having become an embryo, he comes into being there.
t.1.85.12: Does the embryo here fashion another body for itself, or does it go by its own desire as it enters this human womb? Explain this to me, for I ask out of doubt.
t.1.85.13: By what means does it obtain the full growth of body, frame and the rest, its eyes and ears, and consciousness? Being asked, explain this whole truth, dear father, for we all regard you as a knower of the field.
t.1.85.14: In the fertile season the wind draws the seed, mingled with the essence of flowers, up into the womb. There, having taken charge of the subtle elements, it gradually makes the embryo grow in this world.
t.1.85.15: Being born with his limbs formed, the human being becomes the abode in which the six faculties of knowledge are established; here he perceives sound with his two ears and sees every form with his eye.
t.1.85.17: When a man has died and is burned, or buried, or worn away, he has become nonexistent and gone to destruction; by what means, then, does he afterwards become conscious of himself?
t.1.85.16: By the nose one knows smell, by the tongue taste, by the skin touch, and by the mind the inner state. Thus, Aṣṭaka, know this to be the growth here within the body of the great-souled, breathing being.
t.1.85.18: Having given up his life-breaths as if falling asleep, having groaned aloud, and placing before him his good and evil deeds, he leaves the body and, following in the wake of the wind, enters another womb, O lion among kings.
t.1.85.19: Those who do meritorious deeds go to a meritorious womb; those who do evil deeds go to an evil womb. The wicked become worms and insects; I have no wish to speak further, O illustrious one.
t.1.85.21: Aṣṭaka said: By doing what, father, does a mortal obtain the best worlds, by austerity or by knowledge? Since I have asked you, tell me all of it truly: that by which one may go, step by step, to the auspicious worlds.
t.1.85.20: Four-footed, two-footed and six-footed creatures alike come into being in this way, having first become embryos. All this has been told to you in full; what more do you ask, lion among kings?
t.1.85.24: Four acts that make one free from fear bring fear when they are performed improperly: the fire-offering made out of pride, silence kept out of pride, study pursued with pride, and sacrifice offered out of pride.
t.1.85.22: Austerity, charity, tranquility, self-restraint, modesty, uprightness, and compassion for all beings are destroyed by pride, and men overcome by it always fall into darkness; so say the good.
t.1.85.23: He who, while studying the Veda and thinking himself learned, uses his knowledge to destroy the fame of others, finds that his worlds come to an end, and his learning does not grant him the fruit that is brahman.
t.1.85.25: When honored, one should not take delight, nor should one fall into distress from being dishonored. In this world the good honor the good; the wicked do not attain a good understanding.
t.1.85.27: That by which the wise make known the ancient refuge, worshipped with the reverence of the mind: having reached that highest good, that radiant form, they would attain supreme peace, both here and after death.
t.1.85.26: "One should give, one should sacrifice, one should study: this is my vow." In such a declaration, they say, lie things deemed free from fear, yet these are always to be avoided.
